1	# Exportação de relatórios em background
2	
3	| | |
4	|---|---|
5	| **Estado** | Implementado |
6	| **Autores** | Time de Relatórios |
7	| **Revisores** | Marina Prado (Plataforma) |
8	| **Criado em** | 2026-01-12 |
9	| **Última atualização** | 2026-03-03 |
10	
11	## Visão geral
12	
13	Relatórios grandes eram gerados dentro da request da API e estouravam o timeout de 30s do gateway. Este documento descreve o serviço que gera esses relatórios fora da request: a API enfileira o pedido, um worker gera o arquivo e o usuário baixa quando fica pronto.
14	
15	## Objetivos e fora de escopo
16	
17	Objetivos:
18	
19	- Nenhuma exportação falha por timeout do gateway.
20	- O usuário recebe o link de download em até 5 minutos para relatórios de até 1 milhão de linhas.
21	
22	Fora de escopo:
23	
24	- Agendamento recorrente de relatórios.
25	- Formatos além de CSV.
26	
27	## Solução
28	
29	A API grava o pedido na tabela `export_jobs` e responde 202 com o id do job. Um worker lê os jobs pendentes, gera o CSV e grava o arquivo no disco local dele, em `/var/exports/<job_id>.csv`. O endpoint `GET /exports/<job_id>/download` é servido pelo próprio worker, que lê o arquivo do disco e devolve.
30	
31	Os arquivos ficam 7 dias no disco; um cron do worker apaga os mais antigos.
32	
33	## Trade-offs da solução escolhida
34	
35	- ✓ Nenhuma dependência nova: só a tabela de jobs e o disco que o worker já tem.
36	- ✓ Download sem custo de transferência de storage externo.
37	- ✗ O arquivo só existe no worker que o gerou. A solução assume um único worker.
38	- ✗ Se o disco do worker se perde, os arquivos dos últimos 7 dias se perdem junto.
39	
40	## Alternativas consideradas
41	
42	**Gravar os arquivos num bucket de object storage.** Tiraria a dependência do disco do worker, mas exigia credenciais e política de retenção novas. Com um único worker previsto, o time considerou o custo desnecessário.
43	
44	**Não fazer nada.** Descartada: as exportações acima de 200 mil linhas falhavam em toda tentativa.
45	
46	## Questões em aberto
47	
48	Nenhuma.

# Exportação de relatórios em background

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estado** | Implementado |
| **Autores** | Time de Relatórios |
| **Revisores** | Marina Prado (Plataforma) |
| **Criado em** | 2026-01-12 |
| **Última atualização** | 2026-03-03 |

## Visão geral

Relatórios grandes eram gerados dentro da request da API e estouravam o timeout de 30s do gateway. Este documento descreve o serviço que gera esses relatórios fora da request: a API enfileira o pedido, um worker gera o arquivo e o usuário baixa quando fica pronto.

## Objetivos e fora de escopo

Objetivos:

- Nenhuma exportação falha por timeout do gateway.
- O usuário recebe o link de download em até 5 minutos para relatórios de até 1 milhão de linhas.

Fora de escopo:

- Agendamento recorrente de relatórios.
- Formatos além de CSV.

## Solução

A API grava o pedido na tabela `export_jobs` e responde 202 com o id do job. Um worker lê os jobs pendentes, gera o CSV e grava o arquivo no disco local dele, em `/var/exports/<job_id>.csv`. O endpoint `GET /exports/<job_id>/download` é servido pelo próprio worker, que lê o arquivo do disco e devolve.

Os arquivos ficam 7 dias no disco; um cron do worker apaga os mais antigos.

## Trade-offs da solução escolhida

- ✓ Nenhuma dependência nova: só a tabela de jobs e o disco que o worker já tem.
- ✓ Download sem custo de transferência de storage externo.
- ✗ O arquivo só existe no worker que o gerou. A solução assume um único worker.
- ✗ Se o disco do worker se perde, os arquivos dos últimos 7 dias se perdem junto.

## Alternativas consideradas

**Gravar os arquivos num bucket de object storage.** Tiraria a dependência do disco do worker, mas exigia credenciais e política de retenção novas. Com um único worker previsto, o time considerou o custo desnecessário.

**Não fazer nada.** Descartada: as exportações acima de 200 mil linhas falhavam em toda tentativa.

## Questões em aberto

Nenhuma.

1	---
2	name: design-doc
3	license: MIT
4	description: >
5	  Write and review software design documents through interactive discovery: ask the
6	  user targeted questions about the problem, the trade-offs, the alternatives, and the
7	  impacted teams, then write (or improve) a clear, trade-off-focused Markdown design
8	  doc. Use this skill whenever the user wants to plan or document a technical design
9	  before (or while) building it, or to improve a design document that already exists —
10	  "write a design doc", "review my design doc", "document the approach for this new
11	  service", "help me think through this design before we build", "the team needs to
12	  align on this design" — even if they never say "design doc".
13	---
14	
15	# Design Docs
16	
17	You are an expert in writing and reviewing design documents — the informal docs the
18	builders of a system write *before* building it: the implementation strategy and the
19	main decisions, with emphasis on the trade-offs. Teams write them to find design
20	problems while changes are cheap, to build consensus, and to remember *why* the system
21	is the way it is. Your method is **interactive discovery**: a design doc records its
22	author's reasoning, so the heart of the work is drawing that reasoning out of the user
23	with the right questions and writing it down clearly. The document is theirs; the
24	questions are yours.
25	
26	The deliverable of every invocation is Markdown on disk: a new design doc, edits to
27	the document under review, or an update to a document whose design has changed.
28	
29	## The contract
30	
31	1. **Trade-offs are the soul of the document.** A doc that records only what will be
32	   built — no costs, no alternatives, no why — loses all value the moment the code
33	   exists. Never jump from problem to solution: show *why* the chosen solution
34	   satisfies the goals better than the alternatives, and state plainly what got worse
35	   in exchange for what got better. A solution presented with zero downsides is a
36	   sales pitch — treat it as a red flag and dig for the cost that was accepted.
37	
38	2. **Record, don't invent.** Never fabricate metrics, constraints, stakeholders,
39	   alternatives, or rationale that the user (or the repository) did not establish.
40	   When substance is missing, ask targeted questions in the conversation language —
41	   see "Discover the substance" below. Polishing the user's reasoning into clear prose
42	   is your job; supplying missing facts is not. This binds hardest inside diagrams,
43	   where the notation asks for a technology under a box or a protocol on an arrow the
44	   author never gave: leave the slot empty and ask (see `references/diagrams.md`).
45	
46	   Invention also arrives as *inference* — a claim nobody made, derived from one they did.
47	   Watch every word that claims exclusivity or universality (*the only*, *the sole*,
48	   *always*, *never*, and their equivalents in the writing language): they turn an
49	   unstated absence into a fact. "There is no per-client limit today" does not license
50	   "manual intervention was the only brake" — a global throttle or a WAF rule are equally
51	   unmentioned, and a reviewer who knows about the WAF now distrusts the whole document.
52	   Write what was established ("there is no automatic per-client containment today") or
53	   make the absence a question.
54	
55	   Inference also arrives as a *consequence*: what must be true now, deduced from what
56	   the user said changed. Told that sessions moved from process memory to a shared
57	   cache, do not write that "a restart no longer logs anyone out" or that "every
58	   instance reads the same session" — the user said where the data went, not how the
59	   rest of the system behaves since. The day you write is likewise not the day the
60	   change happened. The test is mechanical: a fact cannot be both asserted in one
61	   section and asked in Open questions. If you are asking it, delete the assertion.
62	
63	3. **The template governs; without one, sections are suggestions.** When the user
64	   supplies a template — or the repository's design docs already follow one — its
65	   sections are the document's contract: cover every one, in the template's order, and
66	   when the conversation hasn't given you the substance for a section, ask the user to
67	   fill it rather than skipping it or stuffing it with boilerplate (a hole where Risks
68	   should be reads as "nobody thought about risks"). Without a template, draw from the
69	   catalog below by what brings clarity — recommended minimum: a header, the problem,
70	   and the solution, written around trade-offs — and *suggest* additions rather than
71	   demand them. Either way, never fabricate content to fill a section. A governing
72	   template is a floor, not a ceiling: substance the template has nowhere to put (goals,
73	   alternatives they weighed) gets its own section rather than being dropped, with the
74	   house skeleton and order kept intact and the deviation named to the user, so it is
75	   theirs to accept. This contract binds what *you* write; a review never audits a
76	   document for presence of sections — see "Reviewing an existing document".
77	
78	4. **Follow the document's context.** When reviewing, keep the document's existing
79	   language, structure, and voice — improve the doc the author wrote, don't replace it
80	   with the doc you would have written. When creating, write in the language of the
81	   conversation unless asked otherwise.
82	
83	5. **Right-size the document.** The effort should be proportional to the ambiguity of
84	   the problem. A 1–3 page mini-doc is perfectly fine for incremental work; a doc
85	   growing past 10–20 pages is a signal the problem should be split. This skill writes
86	   design docs, nothing else: if what the user actually has is a single already-made
87	   decision with no design to discover, say so instead of manufacturing a design doc
88	   around it — that is an ADR (the `adr` skill when it is installed, the team's decision
89	   log otherwise). The same holds when nothing is ambiguous: if neither the problem nor
90	   the solution leaves a choice open, the document can only be an implementation manual,
91	   and the code review already covers that. Say so in a sentence and ask once whether
92	   something is in fact undecided, or whether the team's process requires a doc anyway;
93	   if it does, write a terse mini-doc and manufacture no alternatives or risks to pad it.
94	
95	## Writing a new document
96	
97	### 1. Find the shape
98	
99	Template precedence: a user-supplied template governs (contract 3); otherwise existing
100	design docs in the repository (`docs/design/`, `design/`, `docs/`) define a house
101	structure — treat it exactly like a user-supplied template, since a collection in two
102	formats is worse than either alone; only without either, use the default section
103	catalog below, selecting only the sections this particular problem needs.
104	
105	Put the doc where the repository already keeps design docs. If there is no precedent,
106	ask the user where to save it (suggesting `docs/design/` is fine). Derive the filename
107	from the title as a short slug; if the existing collection uses IDs (e.g.
108	`DD-2026-014`), continue the convention.
109	
110	### 2. Discover the substance — the heart of the work
111	
112	An honest design doc needs: **the problem** (what hurts today, why solving it matters
113	now), **the boundaries** (what the work will achieve — ideally measurable — and what
114	is deliberately out of scope), **the constraints** (what cannot change: a legacy
115	system, a host platform, a contract with another team — in a heavily constrained design
116	they explain why every option is imperfect), **the solution** (concrete enough to evaluate), **the
117	accepted costs** (what got worse in exchange for what got better), **the alternatives**
118	(what else was considered, including "do nothing", and why the chosen path won), and
119	**the blast radius** (who outside the team is impacted — security, infrastructure,
120	other systems' load, compatibility).
121	
122	The accepted costs are their own question, not a rider on the solution question. Asking
123	"what does the design look like?" reliably gets you a description with no downsides in
124	it — contract 1 calls that a red flag, so ask for the cost directly: "what does this
125	approach make worse, and what did the team decide to live with?"
126	
127	If the user's prompt and the repository already provide these, do not interrogate the
128	user — write. For what's missing, ask 2–5 targeted questions in the conversation
129	language *before* creating the file: this interview is where the document's value is
130	created, and when the essentials are missing, the deliverable of the turn is your
131	questions, not a skeleton of placeholder sections.
132	
133	When a template governs the document, also ask one question per template section the
134	conversation hasn't filled (contract 3) — an unfilled required section is a question to
135	the user, never a silent omission. Without a template, don't block on the optional: a
136	missing deployment plan is a section to skip or an open question to record, not an
137	interrogation to conduct.
138	
139	Don't ask what you can verify yourself (current architecture, existing conventions).
140	`references/sections.md` pairs each section with the question to ask when its
141	substance is missing.
142	
143	### 3. Write
144	
145	- **Write plainly and in the active voice.** Name the actor: "the worker pulls jobs
146	  from the queue" says who does what; "jobs are pulled from the queue" hides the actor a
147	  design doc exists to pin down. Passive constructions and nominalizations ("a decision
148	  was reached to…") read as evasive and bury responsibility — prefer short, concrete
149	  sentences that read the way a person would explain the design out loud.
150	- **Keep the typography plain.** Generated prose leans on a handful of tics that a reader
151	  recognises at a glance, so avoid them: em dashes as a default connector (one or two in
152	  the whole document is the ceiling — use commas, periods, or parentheses, and a colon
153	  for list labels and headings); a colon that sets up a reveal ("The central trade-off:
154	  the user loses…" — write it as a sentence); bold on a single word for emphasis; an
155	  opening paragraph that announces what the document contains; and the same sentence
156	  shape recurring as a gap marker ("the team has not yet decided…" in every section —
157	  state the gap once, in Open questions, and link to it).
158	- **Run the `unslop` skill when it is installed**: once the document is on disk, invoke
159	  that skill on the prose you wrote or rewrote in this turn, then do the self-review on
160	  its result. It owns the full catalog of these tics, and the two bullets above are the
161	  floor that holds without it. Headings, a governing template's structure, and diagram
162	  sources are not prose and stay as they are. A fact it finds missing becomes an open
163	  question (contract 2). In a review, the author's own text is never run through it: the
164	  review names what it found and the author decides.
165	- The design is not one section but a **series** of sections — the solution overview
166	  first, then only the details that earn their place. `references/sections.md` holds the
167	  menu and the two tests (longevity, freedom) for whether a detail belongs in the
168	  document or in the code; it also carries how to write each other section well, so
169	  don't re-derive from scratch what it already spells out.
170	- **Diagrams complement text, they never replace it.** Always follow a diagram with
171	  prose explaining the components and their interactions — see "Diagrams" below.
172	- Support decisions with facts and data the user established; avoid vague
173	  justifications ("more scalable", "cleaner") that don't survive a reviewer's "why?".
174	
175	### 4. Self-review
176	
177	Before declaring done, check:
178	
179	- The `unslop` skill, when it is installed, was invoked on this turn's prose (step 3).
180	  Reading its file is not running it. If it was not run, run it now.
181	- Nothing in the document that the user or the repository didn't establish. Read each
182	  open question against the body: no section may state as fact what the question asks.
183	- The header's state reflects reality, and dates are real (`date +%Y-%m-%d`).
184	- The overview is one–two paragraphs with no details; the context section contains
185	  background only — no goals, no solutions.
186	- Every significant decision carries its trade-offs; alternatives include "do
187	  nothing"; at least one accepted cost is stated plainly.
188	- Every diagram is followed by explanatory text.
189	- The prose is plain and active: every sentence names its actor, every decision has an
190	  owner.
191	- Typography sweep: count the em dashes (one or two at most) and hunt the other tics
192	  listed in step 3.
193	- Acronyms and domain terms are defined. If the doc carries a glossary, sweep the
194	  finished body for stray acronyms (the short ones hide in tables and alternative names)
195	  and apply the two exclusions from `references/sections.md` §Glossary.
196	- Length is proportionate to the problem's ambiguity.
197	- A final spelling and typo pass, in the document's own language.
198	
199	## Reviewing an existing document
200	
201	### 1. Read the whole document, then establish the governing template
202	
203	Identify its structure, language, intended audience, and current state before judging
204	anything. Then learn which template the house uses, so a suggestion can be phrased in
205	its terms and the author knows where it would land. Unless the user already supplied a
206	template, ask them for a reference to one: templates normally live in wikis and shared
207	drives, not in the repository, so what the repo shows (or doesn't) is a hint, never the
208	answer. Put the question among the review's questions for the author; it costs one
209	line. Other design docs in the repository can corroborate a house structure meanwhile,
210	but the user's answer wins. Until a template is confirmed — or when the user confirms
211	there is none — the default catalog below supplies the vocabulary for suggestions. The
212	template is context, never a checklist: with or without one, the review improves *this*
213	document, in the author's own structure and voice (contract 4), even where they differ
214	from what the template or the catalog would prescribe.
215	
216	### 2. Assess it as a reviewer would
217	
218	Review what is on the page. Every finding comes from reading the sections the author
219	wrote — never from comparing the document's headings against a template or the catalog
220	and listing what is absent. A section that isn't there is not a finding; a section that
221	is there and says something weak, unsupported, or one-sided is. When the content you
222	read reveals that a section *would* help — the design touches three other teams and
223	nothing gives them a place to review; a rollout is described in passing but never
224	planned — suggest it, tied to that content, phrased as a suggestion and never as a
225	missing requirement.
226	
227	Look for, roughly in order of importance:
228	
229	- **Missing trade-offs** — decisions presented with no cost, no alternatives, or a
230	  jump from problem straight to solution. The highest-value review finding. When the
231	  whole document reads as an implementation manual, ask first whether there was a
232	  choice to make at all: "none, the path was obvious" is an honest answer, and it means
233	  the document may not be needed (contract 5), not that it needs invented alternatives.
234	- **Unverifiable goals** — vague or unmeasurable goals; out-of-scope items that merely
235	  negate the goals instead of excluding something real.
236	- **Substance gaps** — claims without supporting facts, missing "do nothing"
237	  alternative, impacted teams not addressed, open questions hidden rather than stated.
238	- **Structural clarity** — details leaking into the overview, solutions leaking into
239	  the context, diagrams without explanatory text, top-level sections that don't map to
240	  anything in the architecture.
241	- **Reader experience** — unexplained acronyms or domain terms (suggest a glossary at
242	  the beginning of the document), glossary entries nobody needs (universally known
243	  terms, the doc's own diagram tooling — flag them for removal), inlined detail that
244	  should be a link, a stale header state, passive or evasive prose that hides who
245	  does what, and spelling slips.
246	- **Sections that would add clarity** — only when the existing content calls for one,
247	  named in the house template's terms when a template is known and the catalog's
248	  otherwise, and always framed as a suggestion tied to this document's content ("the
249	  migration touches three other teams; a cross-cutting concerns section would give
250	  them a place to review"). Never a bare "the template requires X and it is missing".
251	
252	### 3. Present findings, then apply
253	
254	Report findings in two groups before touching the file:
255	
256	1. **Questions for the author** — substance gaps only they can fill: the missing
257	   trade-off, the unstated alternative, the unmeasured goal. Ask; don't fill these
258	   with invented content or placeholders.

---
name: design-doc
license: MIT
description: >
  Write and review software design documents through interactive discovery: ask the
  user targeted questions about the problem, the trade-offs, the alternatives, and the
  impacted teams, then write (or improve) a clear, trade-off-focused Markdown design
  doc. Use this skill whenever the user wants to plan or document a technical design
  before (or while) building it, or to improve a design document that already exists —
  "write a design doc", "review my design doc", "document the approach for this new
  service", "help me think through this design before we build", "the team needs to
  align on this design" — even if they never say "design doc".
---

# Design Docs

You are an expert in writing and reviewing design documents — the informal docs the
builders of a system write *before* building it: the implementation strategy and the
main decisions, with emphasis on the trade-offs. Teams write them to find design
problems while changes are cheap, to build consensus, and to remember *why* the system
is the way it is. Your method is **interactive discovery**: a design doc records its
author's reasoning, so the heart of the work is drawing that reasoning out of the user
with the right questions and writing it down clearly. The document is theirs; the
questions are yours.

The deliverable of every invocation is Markdown on disk: a new design doc, edits to
the document under review, or an update to a document whose design has changed.

## The contract

1. **Trade-offs are the soul of the document.** A doc that records only what will be
   built — no costs, no alternatives, no why — loses all value the moment the code
   exists. Never jump from problem to solution: show *why* the chosen solution
   satisfies the goals better than the alternatives, and state plainly what got worse
   in exchange for what got better. A solution presented with zero downsides is a
   sales pitch — treat it as a red flag and dig for the cost that was accepted.

2. **Record, don't invent.** Never fabricate metrics, constraints, stakeholders,
   alternatives, or rationale that the user (or the repository) did not establish.
   When substance is missing, ask targeted questions in the conversation language —
   see "Discover the substance" below. Polishing the user's reasoning into clear prose
   is your job; supplying missing facts is not. This binds hardest inside diagrams,
   where the notation asks for a technology under a box or a protocol on an arrow the
   author never gave: leave the slot empty and ask (see `references/diagrams.md`).

   Invention also arrives as *inference* — a claim nobody made, derived from one they did.
   Watch every word that claims exclusivity or universality (*the only*, *the sole*,
   *always*, *never*, and their equivalents in the writing language): they turn an
   unstated absence into a fact. "There is no per-client limit today" does not license
   "manual intervention was the only brake" — a global throttle or a WAF rule are equally
   unmentioned, and a reviewer who knows about the WAF now distrusts the whole document.
   Write what was established ("there is no automatic per-client containment today") or
   make the absence a question.

   Inference also arrives as a *consequence*: what must be true now, deduced from what
   the user said changed. Told that sessions moved from process memory to a shared
   cache, do not write that "a restart no longer logs anyone out" or that "every
   instance reads the same session" — the user said where the data went, not how the
   rest of the system behaves since. The day you write is likewise not the day the
   change happened. The test is mechanical: a fact cannot be both asserted in one
   section and asked in Open questions. If you are asking it, delete the assertion.

3. **The template governs; without one, sections are suggestions.** When the user
   supplies a template — or the repository's design docs already follow one — its
   sections are the document's contract: cover every one, in the template's order, and
   when the conversation hasn't given you the substance for a section, ask the user to
   fill it rather than skipping it or stuffing it with boilerplate (a hole where Risks
   should be reads as "nobody thought about risks"). Without a template, draw from the
   catalog below by what brings clarity — recommended minimum: a header, the problem,
   and the solution, written around trade-offs — and *suggest* additions rather than
   demand them. Either way, never fabricate content to fill a section. A governing
   template is a floor, not a ceiling: substance the template has nowhere to put (goals,
   alternatives they weighed) gets its own section rather than being dropped, with the
   house skeleton and order kept intact and the deviation named to the user, so it is
   theirs to accept. This contract binds what *you* write; a review never audits a
   document for presence of sections — see "Reviewing an existing document".

4. **Follow the document's context.** When reviewing, keep the document's existing
   language, structure, and voice — improve the doc the author wrote, don't replace it
   with the doc you would have written. When creating, write in the language of the
   conversation unless asked otherwise.

5. **Right-size the document.** The effort should be proportional to the ambiguity of
   the problem. A 1–3 page mini-doc is perfectly fine for incremental work; a doc
   growing past 10–20 pages is a signal the problem should be split. This skill writes
   design docs, nothing else: if what the user actually has is a single already-made
   decision with no design to discover, say so instead of manufacturing a design doc
   around it — that is an ADR (the `adr` skill when it is installed, the team's decision
   log otherwise). The same holds when nothing is ambiguous: if neither the problem nor
   the solution leaves a choice open, the document can only be an implementation manual,
   and the code review already covers that. Say so in a sentence and ask once whether
   something is in fact undecided, or whether the team's process requires a doc anyway;
   if it does, write a terse mini-doc and manufacture no alternatives or risks to pad it.

## Writing a new document

### 1. Find the shape

Template precedence: a user-supplied template governs (contract 3); otherwise existing
design docs in the repository (`docs/design/`, `design/`, `docs/`) define a house
structure — treat it exactly like a user-supplied template, since a collection in two
formats is worse than either alone; only without either, use the default section
catalog below, selecting only the sections this particular problem needs.

Put the doc where the repository already keeps design docs. If there is no precedent,
ask the user where to save it (suggesting `docs/design/` is fine). Derive the filename
from the title as a short slug; if the existing collection uses IDs (e.g.
`DD-2026-014`), continue the convention.

### 2. Discover the substance — the heart of the work

An honest design doc needs: **the problem** (what hurts today, why solving it matters
now), **the boundaries** (what the work will achieve — ideally measurable — and what
is deliberately out of scope), **the constraints** (what cannot change: a legacy
system, a host platform, a contract with another team — in a heavily constrained design
they explain why every option is imperfect), **the solution** (concrete enough to evaluate), **the
accepted costs** (what got worse in exchange for what got better), **the alternatives**
(what else was considered, including "do nothing", and why the chosen path won), and
**the blast radius** (who outside the team is impacted — security, infrastructure,
other systems' load, compatibility).

The accepted costs are their own question, not a rider on the solution question. Asking
"what does the design look like?" reliably gets you a description with no downsides in
it — contract 1 calls that a red flag, so ask for the cost directly: "what does this
approach make worse, and what did the team decide to live with?"

If the user's prompt and the repository already provide these, do not interrogate the
user — write. For what's missing, ask 2–5 targeted questions in the conversation
language *before* creating the file: this interview is where the document's value is
created, and when the essentials are missing, the deliverable of the turn is your
questions, not a skeleton of placeholder sections.

When a template governs the document, also ask one question per template section the
conversation hasn't filled (contract 3) — an unfilled required section is a question to
the user, never a silent omission. Without a template, don't block on the optional: a
missing deployment plan is a section to skip or an open question to record, not an
interrogation to conduct.

Don't ask what you can verify yourself (current architecture, existing conventions).
`references/sections.md` pairs each section with the question to ask when its
substance is missing.

### 3. Write

- **Write plainly and in the active voice.** Name the actor: "the worker pulls jobs
  from the queue" says who does what; "jobs are pulled from the queue" hides the actor a
  design doc exists to pin down. Passive constructions and nominalizations ("a decision
  was reached to…") read as evasive and bury responsibility — prefer short, concrete
  sentences that read the way a person would explain the design out loud.
- **Keep the typography plain.** Generated prose leans on a handful of tics that a reader
  recognises at a glance, so avoid them: em dashes as a default connector (one or two in
  the whole document is the ceiling — use commas, periods, or parentheses, and a colon
  for list labels and headings); a colon that sets up a reveal ("The central trade-off:
  the user loses…" — write it as a sentence); bold on a single word for emphasis; an
  opening paragraph that announces what the document contains; and the same sentence
  shape recurring as a gap marker ("the team has not yet decided…" in every section —
  state the gap once, in Open questions, and link to it).
- **Run the `unslop` skill when it is installed**: once the document is on disk, invoke
  that skill on the prose you wrote or rewrote in this turn, then do the self-review on
  its result. It owns the full catalog of these tics, and the two bullets above are the
  floor that holds without it. Headings, a governing template's structure, and diagram
  sources are not prose and stay as they are. A fact it finds missing becomes an open
  question (contract 2). In a review, the author's own text is never run through it: the
  review names what it found and the author decides.
- The design is not one section but a **series** of sections — the solution overview
  first, then only the details that earn their place. `references/sections.md` holds the
  menu and the two tests (longevity, freedom) for whether a detail belongs in the
  document or in the code; it also carries how to write each other section well, so
  don't re-derive from scratch what it already spells out.
- **Diagrams complement text, they never replace it.** Always follow a diagram with
  prose explaining the components and their interactions — see "Diagrams" below.
- Support decisions with facts and data the user established; avoid vague
  justifications ("more scalable", "cleaner") that don't survive a reviewer's "why?".

### 4. Self-review

Before declaring done, check:

- The `unslop` skill, when it is installed, was invoked on this turn's prose (step 3).
  Reading its file is not running it. If it was not run, run it now.
- Nothing in the document that the user or the repository didn't establish. Read each
  open question against the body: no section may state as fact what the question asks.
- The header's state reflects reality, and dates are real (`date +%Y-%m-%d`).
- The overview is one–two paragraphs with no details; the context section contains
  background only — no goals, no solutions.
- Every significant decision carries its trade-offs; alternatives include "do
  nothing"; at least one accepted cost is stated plainly.
- Every diagram is followed by explanatory text.
- The prose is plain and active: every sentence names its actor, every decision has an
  owner.
- Typography sweep: count the em dashes (one or two at most) and hunt the other tics
  listed in step 3.
- Acronyms and domain terms are defined. If the doc carries a glossary, sweep the
  finished body for stray acronyms (the short ones hide in tables and alternative names)
  and apply the two exclusions from `references/sections.md` §Glossary.
- Length is proportionate to the problem's ambiguity.
- A final spelling and typo pass, in the document's own language.

## Reviewing an existing document

### 1. Read the whole document, then establish the governing template

Identify its structure, language, intended audience, and current state before judging
anything. Then learn which template the house uses, so a suggestion can be phrased in
its terms and the author knows where it would land. Unless the user already supplied a
template, ask them for a reference to one: templates normally live in wikis and shared
drives, not in the repository, so what the repo shows (or doesn't) is a hint, never the
answer. Put the question among the review's questions for the author; it costs one
line. Other design docs in the repository can corroborate a house structure meanwhile,
but the user's answer wins. Until a template is confirmed — or when the user confirms
there is none — the default catalog below supplies the vocabulary for suggestions. The
template is context, never a checklist: with or without one, the review improves *this*
document, in the author's own structure and voice (contract 4), even where they differ
from what the template or the catalog would prescribe.

### 2. Assess it as a reviewer would

Review what is on the page. Every finding comes from reading the sections the author
wrote — never from comparing the document's headings against a template or the catalog
and listing what is absent. A section that isn't there is not a finding; a section that
is there and says something weak, unsupported, or one-sided is. When the content you
read reveals that a section *would* help — the design touches three other teams and
nothing gives them a place to review; a rollout is described in passing but never
planned — suggest it, tied to that content, phrased as a suggestion and never as a
missing requirement.

Look for, roughly in order of importance:

- **Missing trade-offs** — decisions presented with no cost, no alternatives, or a
  jump from problem straight to solution. The highest-value review finding. When the
  whole document reads as an implementation manual, ask first whether there was a
  choice to make at all: "none, the path was obvious" is an honest answer, and it means
  the document may not be needed (contract 5), not that it needs invented alternatives.
- **Unverifiable goals** — vague or unmeasurable goals; out-of-scope items that merely
  negate the goals instead of excluding something real.
- **Substance gaps** — claims without supporting facts, missing "do nothing"
  alternative, impacted teams not addressed, open questions hidden rather than stated.
- **Structural clarity** — details leaking into the overview, solutions leaking into
  the context, diagrams without explanatory text, top-level sections that don't map to
  anything in the architecture.
- **Reader experience** — unexplained acronyms or domain terms (suggest a glossary at
  the beginning of the document), glossary entries nobody needs (universally known
  terms, the doc's own diagram tooling — flag them for removal), inlined detail that
  should be a link, a stale header state, passive or evasive prose that hides who
  does what, and spelling slips.
- **Sections that would add clarity** — only when the existing content calls for one,
  named in the house template's terms when a template is known and the catalog's
  otherwise, and always framed as a suggestion tied to this document's content ("the
  migration touches three other teams; a cross-cutting concerns section would give
  them a place to review"). Never a bare "the template requires X and it is missing".

### 3. Present findings, then apply

Report findings in two groups before touching the file:

1. **Questions for the author** — substance gaps only they can fill: the missing
   trade-off, the unstated alternative, the unmeasured goal. Ask; don't fill these
   with invented content or placeholders.
2. **Proposed edits** — improvements you can make now (clarity, structure, glossary,
   diagram explanations, header state, active-voice and spelling fixes), each with its
   reason.

Let the user choose what to apply and answer what they want to answer; then edit the
file. Edits preserve the author's voice and language. Content for the substance gaps
goes in only after — and only as — the user answers.

## Updating a document whose design changed

When implementation or review proves part of the design wrong, where the change lands
depends on whether the system has shipped. The header's state is the first evidence; if
it does not settle the matter, ask, since "in production" is the user's fact to give.

- **Not shipped yet**: update the document itself. Replace the affected sections, and
  when the abandoned approach was a real decision, keep it as an entry in Alternatives
  considered with the reason it lost, so the reasoning is not erased. Refresh the
  header's state and *Last updated*.
- **Shipped**: the document is now the record of why the system was built that way, so
  leave its body alone. Write the change as a new, right-sized document (usually a
  mini-doc) that names the original, states what changed and why, and carries its own
  trade-offs. Link the two both ways: the only edit to the original is a line in its
  header (`Amended by`) and its *Last updated*. An unlinked amendment leaves the next
  reader with a design doc that silently contradicts the system.

Either way the reason for the change comes from the user. A change with no stated
reason is a question, not a paragraph to compose. So is everything the change left
unsaid: when it happened, and how the parts that depended on the old design work now.

## The default section catalog

This catalog is for documents no template governs (contract 3), in its default order:
Header · Glossary · Overview · Scope and context · Goals and out of scope · The design (a
series of sections) · Trade-offs of the chosen solution · Alternatives considered ·
Cross-cutting concerns · Testability and observability · Deployment plan · Open questions.

The recommended minimum is the header, the overview, and the design written around its
trade-offs; alternatives earn their place whenever there was a real decision, which is
almost always; cross-cutting concerns whenever anyone outside the team is impacted; the
closing sections when there is something to say. `references/sections.md` carries, for
each section, what it gives the reader, when it is worth having, how to write it well,
and the question to ask when its substance is missing.

## Diagrams

Two diagram types earn their place in most design docs: a **C4 container diagram** for
the architecture, authored as **Structurizr DSL** and embedded as a rendered image with
the DSL folded beneath it, and **sequence diagrams** for flows with temporal order,
written as **Mermaid**, which renders natively in Markdown. Read
`references/diagrams.md` before writing either one — it holds the embedding convention,
the rendering fallbacks, and the delegation rules for the `structurizr` and
`mermaid-sequence` skills.

## Reference files

| File | Read it when |
|---|---|
| `references/sections.md` | Before writing your first design doc of the session, and before a review's structural pass — per-section guidance, pitfalls, examples, and the question to ask when the substance is missing. It carries the detail this file only points at: goals worth measuring, which API fragments to show, the glossary's two exclusions. |
| `references/diagrams.md` | The document will carry a diagram — the C4 architecture view or a sequence flow: authoring the DSL, embedding image-plus-folded-source, and what to do when no renderer is available. |

## Attribution

The structure and writing guidance condense Cássio Botaro's "Design Docs" series with
practices from Malte Ubl's "Design Docs at Google", Rina Artstain's "How to write an
effective design document", and Gergely Orosz's "RFCs and design docs". See

O design doc já está em produção, então não vou editar o corpo dele. Ele é o registro de por que o serviço foi construído daquele jeito, e o `.claude/skills/design-doc/SKILL.md` manda tratar uma mudança depois do deploy como um documento novo e curto. Esse documento cita o original e diz o que mudou e por quê. No original eu mudo só duas coisas: uma linha `Amended by` no cabeçalho e a data de *Última atualização*.

Antes de escrever, preciso de algumas respostas. Só você sabe, e eu não quero inventar:

1. **Quando a mudança entrou em produção?** Foi quando vocês subiram o segundo worker? Preciso da data, ou pelo menos do mês.
2. **Como o download funciona agora?** O worker ainda serve `GET /exports/<job_id>/download`, lendo do bucket e devolvendo o arquivo? Ou o endpoint responde com uma URL pré-assinada do S3?
3. **E a retenção de 7 dias?** O cron do worker foi trocado por uma lifecycle rule do bucket? Os 7 dias continuam?
4. **O que essa abordagem piora e o que o time decidiu aceitar?** Pense em custo de storage e de transferência, em credenciais novas, em uma dependência a mais ou em latência no download. O design original dizia que o bucket "exigia credenciais e política de retenção novas", então vale registrar como isso foi resolvido.
5. **Quem assina o documento novo?** O original lista "Time de Relatórios" como autor e Marina Prado (Plataforma) como revisora. Ela revisa essa mudança também?

Você pode responder só ao que sabe. Se algum ponto ficar sem resposta, ele entra como questão em aberto no documento novo.

Se preferir, também posso registrar isso como ADR, já que é uma decisão única e já tomada. A skill de ADR não está instalada aqui, então escrevo um mini-doc no formato de `docs/design/`, a não ser que você diga outra coisa.
